content.title: About
content.content: The Vanilla Wafer reduced‑fat cookie is a light, crunchy snack made from thin wafer layers flavored with natural vanilla. Each serving contains minimal fat, offering a diet‑friendly alternative to traditional cookies.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cookie is baked with whole‑grain flour, increasing its fiber content.
Part of the butter is replaced by apple puree to lower the fat level while keeping a tender texture.
Vanilla flavor comes from natural extracts, not artificial aromatics.
Thin wafer layers make the cookie airy and quick to digest.
Packaged in a sealed bag that preserves crunch and aroma.

items.title: Low Fat Content
items.content: Reduced fat helps control calorie intake, which is beneficial for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Rich in Fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain flour provides dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Natural Vanilla Aroma
items.content: Vanilla contains antioxidants that may support the immune system.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: The flour and egg white contribute small amounts of vitamins B1, B2 and niacin.

items.title: Energy Boost
items.content: Carbohydrates supply quick energy, making the cookie a convenient snack.

items.title: Gluten Allergy
items.content: Contains wheat, so it is unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar Content
items.content: Despite reduced fat, the cookie contains sugar; diabetics should monitor portion size.

items.title: Choking Hazard for Children
items.content: Thin wafer pieces may pose a choking risk for young children; serve under supervision.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the cookie as a standalone snack, crumble it into yogurt or muesli, or use it as a layer in desserts. For a softer texture, lightly toast it in the oven.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in the original sealed bag. After opening, close the package tightly to prevent moisture absorption. Discard if any moldy odor or off‑flavor develops.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-meat-ns.title: Egg Omelet or Scrambled Egg with Meat

content.title: About
content.content: Egg omelet or scrambled egg with meat is a dish made from beaten eggs mixed with a splash of milk or cream and cooked on a skillet together with pieces of cooked or fried meat (ham, bacon, chicken). The “NS” label refers to the fat type used in preparation, according to the 1992 classification.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs are a complete source of protein, containing all essential amino acids.
Adding meat boosts iron and vitamin B12 content.
The “NS” (non‑standard) fat type denotes the use of fats high in saturated fatty acids.
Omelets can be prepared French‑style (soft, slightly runny) or Russian‑style (firm, fully set).
Traditionally the dish is served with herbs, tomatoes, or bread.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Eggs and meat together provide a high level of biologically available protein, supporting tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish contains vitamins B2, B6 and B12, important for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Meat adds heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Supports eye health
items.content: Egg yolk is rich in lutein and zeaxanthin, antioxidants that protect the eyes.

items.title: Provides sustained energy
items.content: The combination of fats and proteins offers lasting satiety and stable energy levels.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: The NS fat type may raise LDL‑cholesterol when consumed frequently.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals are allergic to eggs, experiencing reactions from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Egg yolks contain cholesterol; people with elevated cholesterol should limit intake.

items.title: Salt and processed meat
items.content: Sausages and bacon often contain high levels of salt and nitrates, which may be undesirable for hypertension.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Beat eggs with a small amount of milk, season with salt and pepper. In a heated skillet with a little NS‑type fat, sauté diced meat, then pour in the egg mixture. Cook, stirring, until desired consistency is reached. Optionally add herbs, cheese, or vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best enjoyed fresh. If needed, store in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 24 hours. Reheat in a skillet or microwave, adding a bit of oil to prevent drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Lard is animal fat rendered from the subcutaneous layer of pigs. It is widely used in many cuisines as a source of energy, flavor, and texture. Lard has a mild, slightly buttery taste and can be found fresh or smoked.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lard is a traditional ingredient in Russian, Ukrainian, and Polish cooking for frying, roasting, and sausage making.
Smoked lard acquires a distinctive aroma through prolonged exposure to smoke.
In some regions lard is considered a delicacy and served thinly sliced with bread and garlic.
Lard can be salted, marinated, or simply dried for long‑term storage.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Lard is calorie‑dense and provides quick energy, which is especially valuable in cold climates.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Lard contains vitamins B1, B2, and B12, essential for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Fat‑soluble vitamins
items.content: Lard provides vitamin D and vitamin E, supporting skin health and immunity.

items.title: Hormone balance support
items.content: Saturated fatty acids in lard participate in hormone synthesis.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Lard is very calorie‑rich, so consumption should be moderate, especially for those managing weight.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: A large amount of saturated fat may contribute to elevated cholesterol levels when eaten frequently.

items.title: Salt and preservatives
items.content: Salted and smoked lard often contains added salt and nitrites, which should be limited.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Lard can be fried, roasted, added to soups and stews, or used for making pâtés and sausages. Thinly sliced cold lard is often served with bread, onion, and vinegar. It can also be melted and used as a flavorful cooking oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store lard in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 2‑3 weeks. For longer storage, freeze it in a vacuum‑sealed bag for up to 6 months. Fresh lard should have no off‑odors or mold.

content.title: About
content.content: Sausage NFS is a ready‑to‑eat meat product made from a blend of beef, pork and spices. The product is thermally processed and vacuum‑packed, providing a long shelf life without added preservatives.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: NFS stands for “No Further Seasoning”, meaning the product is ready to eat without additional seasoning.
The sausage is produced using a traditional recipe combined with modern vacuum‑packaging technology.
It is popular among hikers and for outdoor events because of its convenient transportability.
Only natural ingredients are used, with no artificial colourings.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: The sausage provides high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Meat products are a good source of heme iron, supporting normal blood formation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamins B12, B6 and niacin, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: Provides a quick source of calories, useful during periods of high physical activity.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to the product’s ingredients.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The sausage contains a notable amount of salt; people with hypertension should limit intake.

items.title: Preservatives and nitrites
items.content: Certain batches may contain nitrite additives, which should be consumed in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sausage can be eaten straight from the pack, sliced for sandwiches, added to salads, or briefly pan‑fried. When heating, use moderate heat to avoid drying out the product.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 0 °C to +4 °C. Once opened, consume within 3–5 days. For longer storage, it can be frozen at –18 °C.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken noodle soup is a ready‑to‑eat product containing chicken broth, noodles, pieces of chicken meat and vegetables. It can be quickly heated in a microwave or on the stove, providing a hearty and nutritious meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The soup is often sold in single‑serve packets that are convenient for storage and transport.
Noodles are usually made from wheat flour, though rice or buckwheat varieties are also used.
Chicken broth forms the base of most traditional Asian and European soups.
Typical soups include carrots, onion and celery for added flavor and vitamins.
In some regions spices such as ginger or garlic are added to boost aroma.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Chicken provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair and maintenance.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The broth and meat contain vitamin B6 and niacin, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: The soup supplies potassium, phosphorus and magnesium, important for heart and nerve function.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Warm broth and soft noodles are gentle on the digestive system.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The large liquid volume helps maintain the body’s water balance.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Ready‑made soups often contain high levels of salt; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Wheat noodles may trigger reactions in individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some versions include additives for extended shelf life, which may not suit everyone.

items.title: Thermal safety
items.content: Insufficiently heated soup can harbor bacteria; ensure it reaches a rolling boil.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the packet in the microwave for 2–3 minutes or bring to a boil on the stove, stirring occasionally. Optionally garnish with fresh herbs, pepper or lime to enhance flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep unopened packets in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, consume within 2–3 days and store in a sealed container in the refrigerator.

tea-iced-instant-black-pre-sweetened-wit.title: Tea, iced, instant, black, pre‑sweetened with sugar

content.title: About
content.content: Tea, iced, instant, black, pre‑sweetened with sugar is a ready‑to‑drink beverage that dissolves quickly in cold water. It is made from selected black tea leaves processed for instant solubility and contains added sugar for a sweet taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Black tea contains more caffeine than green tea, making it a good energy boost.
Instant tea was invented in the early 20th century and quickly became popular for its convenience.
Sweetening with sugar makes the drink sweeter but also raises its calorie content.
Iced instant tea is often used in summer cocktails and desserts.
The instant‑soluble technology involves extraction, concentration, and freeze‑drying.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Black tea is rich in polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Improves concentration
items.content: Caffeine in tea can enhance alertness and focus.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Flavonoids may contribute to better vessel function.

items.title: Provides quick energy
items.content: Sugar offers an immediate source of energy.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The beverage helps maintain fluid balance, especially in hot weather.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Excessive intake can lead to weight gain and elevated blood glucose levels.

items.title: Caffeine
items.content: Large amounts may cause nervousness, insomnia, and rapid heartbeat.

items.title: Tea allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to tea components.

items.title: Tooth enamel erosion
items.content: Sugar and acids in the drink can contribute to enamel wear with frequent consumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: To prepare, dissolve a sachet (or measured dry portion) in 200‑250 ml of cold water and stir until fully dissolved. Ice, lemon, or mint can be added for flavor variation.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the package tightly sealed to prevent moisture absorption.

turnip-greens-fresh-cooked-no-added-fat.title: Turnip greens, fresh, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Turnip greens are the edible leaves of the turnip plant, commonly prepared by brief boiling without added fat. The leaves have a mild, slightly bitter flavor and a tender texture. They can be served as a side dish, added to soups, stews, and salads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turnip greens belong to the Brassicaceae family, the same as broccoli and cabbage.
The bright green color comes from a high chlorophyll content.
In many cuisines, especially in the United States and Japan, turnip greens are a seasonal favorite.
Turnip greens grow well in cool climates and can be harvested multiple times per season.
Historically, turnip greens were used in folk medicine to aid digestion.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Turnip greens provide a high amount of vitamin K, essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of vitamin A and carotenoids
items.content: Beta‑carotene in turnip greens converts to vitamin A, supporting vision and immune function.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C offers antioxidant protection and enhances iron absorption.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: Turnip greens supply calcium, magnesium, and iron, important for bones, muscles, and blood formation.

items.title: Low‑calorie fiber source
items.content: Dietary fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and supports a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Turnip greens contain oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: A small number of people may be allergic to cruciferous vegetables, including turnip greens.

items.title: Potential contamination
items.content: Like other leafy greens, turnip greens can retain pesticide residues; thorough washing before cooking is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Turnip greens are typically boiled for 2–4 minutes in salted water without added fat, then shocked in ice water to preserve color and nutrients. They can be served plain, tossed into soups, omelets, pasta, or used in salads after cooling.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh turnip greens keep in the refrigerator wrapped in a damp paper towel or in a sealed container for 3–5 days. Cooked greens should be stored in an airtight container in the fridge and consumed within 2 days.
